summary: Decision support, autonomy, and ISR processing are the programs of record; DIU is the commercial on-ramp. Who tracks the sector: free government procurement databases are the primary record, with dedicated defense-intelligence firms layered on top - this page starts with the sources anyone can verify.

analysis.body:
These sources do not include a Census adoption figure or any measured adoption rate for AI in defense. What they provide instead is a map of procurement systems and commercial entry points. Per DIU, the Defense Innovation Unit is the Department's innovation pointman, with a mission to convert entrepreneurial products into tangible combat power, and it is where commercial AI enters DoD programs.

On deployment, Govini describes a platform layer that transforms activated data into adaptive workflows, mobilized agents, and AI-driven orchestration that proactively forecasts issues, prioritizes recommendations, and aligns resources. Janes states it applies advanced technology to connect millions of data points to uncover patterns, signals, and trajectories, moving from what happened to what it means. Per The World of AI, state-funded government labs such as Technology Innovation Institute and Shanghai AI Laboratory carry public mandates, draw on sovereign budgets, and can command infrastructure commitments including compute and facilities, though these are not presented as U.S. defense programs.

Vendors and money concentrate in federal procurement records. SAM.gov is the primary record of solicitations, and USAspending carries every federal award, downloadable and built on the FPDS feed. FPDS records DoD contract actions and vendor performance history at the transaction level. Govini builds decision science on that record, tracking procurement trends, supply-chain risk, and vendor capability in AI and autonomy, and publishes public scorecards on critical-technology spending. Silicon Valley Defense Group maps the commercial entrants and companies driving AI adoption in the DoD space.

None of these sources reports ROI evidence or quantified returns from AI deployments. Govini claims proactive forecasting and prioritization, and Janes claims decision-grade intelligence, but neither provides a return-on-investment figure in the material gathered here.

On risk and regulatory posture, SAM.gov states the system is a U.S. General Services Administration federal computer system for official use only, subject to monitoring, and that unauthorized activities are subject to disciplinary action including criminal prosecution. It also states the system contains Controlled Unclassified Information, and all individuals viewing, reproducing, or disposing of this information are required to protect it in accordance with 32 CFR Part 2002 and GSA Order CIO 2103.2 CUI Policy. For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the free federal procurement data in SAM.gov, USAspending, and FPDS is the starting point for solicitations, awards, and vendor performance, DIU is the commercial on-ramp, and subscription analysts like Janes and Govini are labeled as such for decision support.

https://www.janes.com/.brief: Janes reports that it gathers information from vetted on-ground specialists, exclusive interviews, and events, acting as human sensors that web crawlers cannot reach. Janes reports that every data point is verified against reliable, vetted sources and that its dataset is the largest of its type, connecting millions of points to uncover patterns. Janes reports that its final content is peer reviewed to meet its quality and accuracy standards, and that it supplies validated data for the Joint Intelligence Preparation of the Operational Environment process. Janes reports that its digital portal lets users navigate validated data to uncover insights, moving from “what happened” to “what it means.”

https://www.govini.com/.brief: Govini says that Air is a leader in Enterprise Readiness and that its mission is to make readiness a real-time, continuously achieved condition. The company explains that its platform layer turns activated data into adaptive workflows, mobilized agents, and AI-driven orchestration that forecasts issues, prioritizes recommendations, and aligns resources.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/ec.brief: According to The World of AI, two government labs are listed: the Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi and Shanghai AI Laboratory in China. Both are state-funded, carry public mandates, and rely on sovereign budgets rather than venture capital, which shapes their research priorities. The Abu Dhabi lab operates under the Advanced Technology Research Council and has released frontier open models, while the Shanghai lab is backed by national ministries and the Shanghai municipal government, aligning it with China’s central research agenda. Each lab can command infrastructure commitments, such as compute and facilities, that market-driven labs must negotiate for commercially. The page also notes that these entries are individually verified, rebuilt daily from primary sources, and lists books by Stephen R. Jordan.
